messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond was fifty years old, a musician who had spent decades playing bass in small clubs and recording studios across the city, when the stalking began. It started with a single persistent fan who appeared at every gig, stood too close to the stage, and sent messages that shifted from admiring to possessive to threatening over the course of eight weeks. The police were called three times. Each time, they told Raymond there was not enough evidence for a restraining order, that the messages were vague, that the man had a right to be in public places. Raymond remembered the night it ended with a clarity that was not really clarity at all — he remembered the feeling of the man’s hand on his arm outside the venue, the cold air, the sound of his own voice shouting, the headlights of a passing car. But there were gaps too. He could not recall how he got from the alley to his apartment. He could not remember whether he had locked the door. The fragments that came back to him arrived without warning — the smell of cigarette smoke, the weight of a hand, the yellow light of a streetlamp — and then vanished just as quickly, leaving him disoriented and trembling. When the memory was fully present, it was not a memory at all but a reliving: every sound, every sensation, every second of terror flooding back as though the alley were right there in his living room.

In the months that followed, Raymond’s world contracted. He stopped taking new gigs in parts of the city he did not know well. Unfamiliar places felt impossible to navigate because he could not see the danger in advance — he could not scan a room he had never been in, could not know where the exits were, could not tell which faces were safe. At the few venues he still played, he found himself watching the audience not for appreciation but for threat. He studied the way people held themselves, the direction of their gaze, the speed of their movements. He became certain that he could spot the one who would harm him, if only he watched closely enough. Nighttime was the worst. Darkness stripped away his ability to see who was coming, and he had come to believe that danger lived in the hours after sunset. He stayed awake long into the night, sitting by the window of his apartment, watching the street below. Sleep came in shallow increments, if it came at all.

The numbness that settled over him was harder to name than the fear. He felt hollow, dead inside, as though the person he had been before — the musician who loved the chaos of a crowded room, who thrived on the unpredictability of live performance — had been replaced by something mechanical. He told himself he was weak. A stronger person would have handled it differently, would have fought back, would have moved on. The institutions that were supposed to protect him had not, and that failure had become a fixed point in his understanding of the world: there was no safety to be found in systems, in laws, in other people. His divorce, which had happened two years before the stalking, now felt like part of the same pattern — a confirmation that he could not rely on anyone to keep him safe.

His career had eroded quietly. He stopped answering calls from promoters who booked unfamiliar venues. He turned down a steady weekly residency because it required him to drive home after midnight. His income dropped, and he spent more and more time alone in his apartment, playing scales on an unamplified bass so as not to draw attention. What finally brought him to seek help was not the fear or the lost work, but the realization that he could no longer remember what it felt like to want anything. He came to the clinic because he hoped — though he was not sure he believed it — that somewhere inside the deadness, the person he used to be was still there, waiting to be found.
